title: Macaque 217 — group-housed rhesus: chronic diarrhoea and weight loss
presentation: Adult female rhesus macaque in a group of fourteen, three months of intermittent diarrhoea with 12% weight loss. Two other animals in the group have looser faeces than normal.

stages.title: Assess the animal and the group
stages.briefing: Weight 6.2 kg, down from 7.0 kg. Reduced muscle mass over the hindquarters, coat in poor condition, mild peripheral oedema. Faeces loose to watery, intermittently with mucus, no frank blood. Appetite variable. Group: fourteen animals, two others with loose faeces, recent reshuffle of group membership after an aggression episode. Enclosure shared water sources; enrichment feeding on the ground.

options.label: Chronic diarrhoea with 12% weight loss and peripheral oedema
options.detail: Protein loss through the gut

options.label: Two further animals in the group with loose faeces
options.detail: Transmissible, or shared environmental exposure

options.label: Recent group reshuffle with an aggression episode
options.detail: Social stress precipitates enteric disease in macaques

options.label: Ground feeding on shared enrichment
options.detail: A plausible route — husbandry, not a clinical sign

options.label: Poor coat condition
options.detail: Follows chronic disease of any kind

stages.explanation: Oedema alongside chronic diarrhoea is the finding that turns this from a nuisance into a protein-losing enteropathy, and the group pattern makes it a colony problem. Social stress after a reshuffle is a genuine precipitant in macaques rather than a soft explanation — it changes what you recommend about group management as well as what you prescribe.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: The macaque is anaesthetised for a full work-up, and group faecal sampling is possible.

options.label: Faecal culture for Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella and Yersinia
options.detail: The bacterial causes of macaque colitis

options.label: Faecal parasitology including Cryptosporidium and Giardia
options.detail: Protozoa are common and treatable

options.label: Serum albumin and total protein
options.detail: Confirms and grades the protein loss

options.label: Colonoscopy with mucosal biopsies for histopathology
options.detail: Distinguishes chronic idiopathic colitis from infection

options.label: Group faecal screening of all fourteen animals
options.detail: Finds carriers and defines the outbreak

options.label: Tuberculin skin testing as the only investigation
options.detail: Essential colony surveillance, but it does not explain a protein-losing colitis

options.label: Barium follow-through as the first-line test
options.detail: Little added value when biopsies are available

stages.explanation: Chronic macaque diarrhoea needs both an infectious search and biopsies, because chronic idiopathic colitis is a diagnosis of exclusion and histology is how you exclude. Screening the group is what turns an individual case into colony management. Tuberculosis surveillance matters enormously in primate collections and is a parallel programme rather than this diagnosis.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Faecal culture: Campylobacter jejuni isolated from this animal and from four of fourteen group members, two of them clinically normal; Shigella, Salmonella and Yersinia not isolated. Parasitology: no Cryptosporidium, no Giardia, light Trichuris burden. Albumin 21 g/L (low), total protein 48 g/L (low). Colonoscopy: diffusely granular, friable colonic mucosa; histopathology shows chronic lymphoplasmacytic colitis with crypt loss and no acid-fast organisms. Tuberculin test negative.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Chronic colitis with protein loss
options.detail: Histology plus an albumin of 21 g/L

options.label: Campylobacter jejuni is circulating in the group, including in carriers
options.detail: Isolated from five animals, two without signs

options.label: The mucosal damage is chronic rather than acute
options.detail: Crypt loss with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate

options.label: Tuberculosis is excluded on current testing
options.detail: Negative tuberculin test and no acid-fast organisms on biopsy

options.label: Trichuris is the primary cause
options.detail: A light burden does not produce crypt loss and hypoalbuminaemia

options.label: Cryptosporidiosis explains the group picture
options.detail: Not detected on parasitology

stages.explanation: Campylobacter with chronic lymphoplasmacytic colitis is the typical macaque picture: the organism is part of the story and the chronic mucosal change is what keeps the animal thin. Carriers with no signs are why treating one animal fails. The negative tuberculosis results are worth stating explicitly in a primate colony record, because that question is asked of every case.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Campylobacter jejuni from five of fourteen animals including two carriers, chronic lymphoplasmacytic colitis with crypt loss, albumin 21 g/L, light Trichuris burden, tuberculosis negative.

options.label: Chronic colitis with protein-losing enteropathy, associated with group Campylobacter and social stress
options.detail: The lesion, the protein loss, the organism and the trigger

options.label: Acute campylobacteriosis
options.detail: Understates three months of colitis with crypt loss

options.label: Trichuriasis
options.detail: A light burden with the wrong lesion

options.label: Intestinal tuberculosis
options.detail: Excluded on testing and histology

options.label: Gastrointestinal lymphoma
options.detail: Histology shows inflammation, not neoplasia

stages.explanation: A diagnosis in four clauses gives a plan in four parts: treat this animal and the carriers, support the protein loss nutritionally, manage the mucosal inflammation, and address the social and feeding arrangements that drive both stress and faecal-oral spread. Colony medicine rewards diagnoses written at group level.
